Kotlin Multiplatform, from the compiler up · check

Know One codebase, two worlds already?

One question for each of the 7 puzzles in this module. A right answer marks that puzzle as passed, so you can jump ahead. A wrong one tells you which puzzle to start with. Nothing is sent anywhere: it's saved in this browser.

Puzzle 0: One Kotlin function, two ways to run it

Your Android build has produced Kotlin class files, then stops before making DEX. Which step is still missing before those classes can run as part of the app?

Not quite. Kotlin/Native is the iOS path here. The Android build produces the DEX. Learn it in puzzle 0 →

Not quite. ART runs DEX on the phone. It gets the DEX that the build produced. Learn it in puzzle 0 →

Right. Follow the output of the build up to the moment it reaches the phone.

Puzzle 1: What every target has

You call java.io.File in commonMain, and the project has Android and iOS targets. What happens when you build for iOS?

Not quite. Common code is compiled for every target; on iOS it can't compile at all. Learn it in puzzle 1 →

Not quite. Kotlin/Native compiles your Kotlin; it can't bring along a Java library the iPhone doesn't have. Learn it in puzzle 1 →

Right. Common code may only use what every target has.

Puzzle 2: How Kotlin calls Apple

Why does import platform.UIKit.UIDevice fail in commonMain?

Right. Apple bindings, Apple targets only.

Not quite. Common code can use libraries built for every target. Learn it in puzzle 2 →

Not quite. Size isn't the issue; Android has no UIKit at all. Learn it in puzzle 2 →

Puzzle 3: A promise and its keepers

You add a web target. platformName() has actuals for Android and iOS only. What happens?

Not quite. There's no default: the compiler requires an actual for every target. Learn it in puzzle 3 →

Right. Every target must keep the promise.

Not quite. One platform's actual is never used for another; each target needs its own. Learn it in puzzle 3 →

Puzzle 4: An iOS app in one puzzle

Which iOS piece plays the role of an Activity?

Right. One screen, one view controller.

Not quite. UIKit is the framework; a view controller is one screen built with it. Learn it in puzzle 4 →

Not quite. Xcode is the IDE; it builds the app, it isn't part of it. Learn it in puzzle 4 →

Puzzle 5: How Swift sees your Kotlin

The iOS team opens this Objective-C-exported framework in Xcode. What do they read to learn your API?

Not quite. The framework holds native code and an Objective-C description; Swift never reads Kotlin. Learn it in puzzle 5 →

Right. Swift learns your API from the Objective-C header.

Not quite. Kotlin describes your code in Objective-C, not Swift; Swift reads that. Learn it in puzzle 5 →

Puzzle 6: Lost in translation

Your shared code exposes a Flow<User>. What does Swift see?

Not quite. Generics cross only on classes; Flow is an interface, so its type parameter is lost. Learn it in puzzle 6 →

Right. Interface generics are lost in the Objective-C header.

Not quite. The Flow does cross, as an Objective-C type; only its type parameter is lost. Learn it in puzzle 6 →
